title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Silver Ticket
shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Silver Ticket
summary: A silver ticket is a forged ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket, also called a service ticket, created with the password hash of the account that runs a specific service. The ticket is encrypted with that service account key, so the service receiving it can validate it without asking the Key Distribution Center (KDC) for confirmation. That is the key difference from a golden ticket: no domain controller interaction is needed, so no Kerberos event appears on a domain controller when the ticket is used. Scope is also narrower, because the forged ticket only works against the targeted service and the host running it, such as a database, a file share or a web application. Detection is hard for that reason and usually depends on host and service logs rather than domain controller logs: service logons where the client address is unrelated to the account, service access at unusual hours or from unusual hosts, and audit records showing network authentication without a matching TGS request anywhere. The nearest legitimate pattern is a cached service session, so the account's normal working hosts and times form the baseline.

beginner.definition: A silver ticket is a fake service ticket made with the password hash of one service account. A service ticket is what Kerberos gives you for a single resource, such as a file share or a database. Because the service can check the ticket by itself, the attacker never needs to speak to the domain controller. This sub-technique differs from a golden ticket: it reaches less, but it is harder to see.
beginner.whyItMatters: A silver ticket gives access to one service without any domain controller conversation. That means the central logs may show nothing at all. An attacker can use it to read a database or change files, and the service simply accepts the request. It also survives a password change on the user account, because the ticket is tied to the service account instead. If you only monitor domain controllers, this activity can sit in your network unseen.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains the password hash of the account that runs a chosen service.
That hash is the key the service itself uses to check incoming tickets.
The attacker builds a service ticket offline and signs it with that hash.
They put whatever username or group membership they want inside that ticket.
The ticket is presented straight to the service, with no request to the domain controller.
The service accepts it, giving access limited to that one resource and its host.
beginner.example: Imagine a staff canteen where the till checks a stamp on each lunch voucher. The stamp is made with a small stamping tool that is kept in the kitchen. If someone copies that tool, they can print vouchers at home. The till accepts every voucher, because the stamp looks right, and head office never hears about it. The fraud only covers lunches, not the whole building, so the damage is smaller than with a copied master key. It is invisible unless the canteen compares vouchers with the lunches it actually served.
takeaways: Long random passwords for service accounts make forged service tickets much harder.
Monitor service hosts, not only domain controllers, for unexpected logons.
Group managed service accounts rotate their passwords automatically, which helps here.

objectives: Explain how a service ticket is validated by the service rather than by the domain controller.
Describe how the hash of a service account enables offline service ticket forgery.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from a golden ticket in scope and in visibility.
Identify the service host and domain controller records that could reveal forged tickets.
Recommend service account practices that make ticket forgery impractical.
